hmmt-feb-2003-comb-01.title: Everything must be equal
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-01.body:
All switches end ON exactly when every switch has two neighbours (initially) in the same position, i.e. switch $i-1$ and $i+1$ agree for all $i$. Because $2003$ is odd, stepping by $2$ around the circle visits every switch ($1,3,5,\ldots,2003,2,4,\ldots,2002$), so all $2003$ switches must have been initially in the same position. That is $2$ configurations out of $2^{2003}$, a probability of $\frac2{2^{2003}}=\frac1{2^{2002}}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{2^{2002}}$**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-02.title: Rows and blocks
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-02.body:
Think of the grid as $10$ rows of $2$ squares. The two squares in a row are adjacent, so each row has at most one marked square; with nine marks, exactly one row is empty. In any block of consecutive non-empty rows, adjacent rows must use different columns, so the whole block is determined by its first row (2 choices).

- Empty row at an end (2 choices of end): the remaining $9$ rows form one block, so $2$ ways, giving $2\cdot2=4$.
- Empty row in the interior (8 choices): two blocks, $2\cdot2=4$ ways each, giving $8\cdot4=32$.

Total $4+32=36$.

**Answer: 36**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-02.title: Recursive count
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-02.body: Let $a_k$ be the number of ways to fill a block of $k$ rows (one mark each, no vertical adjacency): $a_k=2$ for $k\ge1$ and $a_0=1$. Choosing the empty row $j$ ($1\le j\le10$) gives $a_{j-1}a_{10-j}$ ways: $j=1,10$ give $2$ each, $j=2,\ldots,9$ give $4$ each. Total $2\cdot2+8\cdot4=36$.

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-03.title: Two points at a time
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-03.body:
Look at the game in blocks of two points. In a block Daniel wins both with probability $\left(\frac35\right)^2=\frac9{25}$, Scott wins both with probability $\frac4{25}$, and they split ($\frac{12}{25}$) and return to par. The game ends exactly at the first block that is not a split, and then Daniel wins with probability $\frac{9/25}{9/25+4/25}=\frac9{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{13}$**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-03.title: Equation for $p$
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-03.body: Let $p$ be Daniel's winning probability from par. After two points he has won with probability $\frac9{25}$, lost with $\frac4{25}$, or is back at par with $\frac{12}{25}$, so $p=\frac9{25}+\frac{12}{25}p$, giving $p=\frac{9/25}{13/25}=\frac9{13}$.

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-04.title: Weights
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-04.body:
Give each senator-membership $1$ point and each aide-membership $\frac14$ point. Senators: $100\cdot5=500$ points. Aides: $400\cdot3\cdot\frac14=300$ points. Total $800$. Each type of committee is worth exactly $5$ points: $5$ senators give $5$; $4$ senators and $4$ aides give $4+\frac44=5$; $2$ senators and $12$ aides give $2+\frac{12}4=5$. So there are $\frac{800}5=160$ committees.

**Answer: 160**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-05.title: Odd versus even
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-05.body:
The condition says no odd number shares a color with an even number. So the set of colors used on odds and the set used on evens are disjoint. Colorings where odds use only color $X$ (one color for all five odds): choose $X$ in $3$ ways, then each of the $5$ evens uses one of the other two colors: $3\cdot2^5=96$. Symmetrically, evens all one color: $96$. Both at once (odds all one color, evens all one color): $3\cdot2=6$, counted twice. But we must also consider colorings where neither side is monochrome: then each side uses at least two colors, requiring at least $4$ colors, impossible. So the total is $96+96-6=186$.

**Answer: 186**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-06.title: Checkerboard colouring
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-06.body:
Colour the $35$ chairs like a checkerboard with the corners in the majority colour: there are $18$ red chairs and $17$ black ones, and the centre chair is black. Then all $18$ red chairs are occupied. Each student moves to a chair of the opposite colour, so the $18$ students on red chairs need $18$ distinct black chairs, but only $17$ exist. So no reassignment is possible: $0$ ways.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-07.title: Sum over boxes
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-07.body:
The events \"box $n$ has at least $2$ balls\" are mutually exclusive (there are only $3$ balls), so add their probabilities. For box $n$ with $p=2^{-n}$: $3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3=\frac3{4^n}-\frac2{8^n}$. Summing over $n\ge1$: $\frac{3/4}{1-1/4}-\frac{2/8}{1-1/8}=1-\frac27=\frac57$.

**Answer: $\frac57$**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-08.title: Count pairs $(S,n)$
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-08.body:
For a fixed $n$ and $|S|=k$, $n$ and $n+k$ lie in $S$ (needs $k\ge2$ and $n+k\le15$), and the other $k-2$ elements come from the remaining $13$ numbers: $\binom{13}{k-2}$ sets. So $n$ is an anchor of $\sum_{k=2}^{15-n}\binom{13}{k-2}=\sum_{j=0}^{13-n}\binom{13}j$ sets. The total number of anchors over all subsets is $A=\sum_{n=1}^{13}\sum_{j=0}^{13-n}\binom{13}j=\sum_{j=0}^{12}(13-j)\binom{13}j$. By the symmetry $j\leftrightarrow13-j$, $2A=\sum_{j=0}^{13}13\binom{13}j=13\cdot2^{13}$ (the $j=13$ term has weight $0$ and the paired $j=0$ term completes the sum), so $A=13\cdot2^{12}$. Dividing by the $2^{15}$ subsets gives $\frac{13\cdot2^{12}}{2^{15}}=\frac{13}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{13}8$**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-08.title: Check by enumeration
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-08.body: Verified independently by direct enumeration of all $2^{15}$ subsets: the total number of anchors is $53248=13\cdot4096$, so the average is $\frac{13}8$.

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-09.title: Subsets of clubs
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-09.body:
Identify each student with the set of clubs they belong to, a subset of the $10$ clubs. The two-student condition says these subsets are distinct.

Upper bound. With at least two students some student has a nonempty set $S$. Pair each subset $T$ with $T\triangle S$ (the clubs in exactly one of $S,T$). Since $S
e\emptyset$ this splits the $2^{10}$ subsets into $512$ pairs, and $S$ is paired with $\emptyset$. Take any other pair $\{T,T\triangle S\}$. The sets $S,T,T\triangle S$ are distinct, and every club belongs to an even number (zero or two) of them, so no club contains exactly one or all three of them. Hence no three students can have sets $S,T,T\triangle S$, so at most one of $T,T\triangle S$ is a student's set. This allows at most $1$ ($S$) $+\ 1$ ($\emptyset$) $+\ 511$ (the other pairs) $=513$ students.

Construction. Pick a club $c$. Take one student who belongs to no club, and $512$ students who all belong to $c$ and to the $512$ different subsets of the other $9$ clubs. Any two students are separated by some club. For three students: if all are in $c$, then $c$ contains all three; otherwise one of them is the club-less student, and a club separating the other two contains exactly one of the three. So $513$ is attainable.

**Answer: 513**

hmmt-feb-2003-comb-10.title: Probability of hitting a given value
hmmt-feb-2003-comb-10.body:
Claim: starting from $N$, the probability that a given $M<N$ ever appears is $\frac1{M+1}$. Induct on $N$. For $N=M+1$, $M$ appears iff the first press gives $M$, probability $\frac1N=\frac1{M+1}$. For $N>M+1$: with probability $\frac1N$ the first press gives $N-1$, after which $M$ appears with probability $\frac1{M+1}$ (induction); otherwise (probability $\frac{N-1}N$) the first press is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,N-2\}$, exactly the first press from $N-1$, so $M$ appears with probability $\frac1{M+1}$ again. So the total is $\frac1{M+1}$.

The events chain (the probability of seeing $M$ given that we see $N$ is the same as starting at $N$), so the required probability is $\frac1{1001}\cdot\frac1{101}\cdot\frac1{11}\cdot\frac12=\frac1{2224222}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{2224222}$**
